name: Hotel Front Desk
description: Practice checking in, asking about the hotel, reporting a problem and checking out.

objectives.description: Open the check-in and say they have a reservation.
success_indicators: states the purpose without being asked a leading question
confirms nights, room type or dates correctly

objectives.description: Give their name and any details the desk asks for.
success_indicators: spells a name or gives a number when asked

objectives.description: Ask a question about the room.
success_indicators: asks about floor, view, bed, or quietness

objectives.description: Ask when and where breakfast is.
success_indicators: asks a time question and understands the answer

objectives.description: Ask about internet access and understand the reply.
success_indicators: asks for and repeats back a password or code
asks the time and confirms it

objectives.description: Ask how to find something in the hotel.
success_indicators: asks where something is and follows the answer

objectives.description: Report a problem with the room.
success_indicators: asks for it to be fixed
opens the check-out and returns the key

objectives.description: Query or confirm the charges and pay.

teaching_philosophy: Be the receptionist: polite, efficient, slightly formal.
This scenario is full of numbers and spellings. Use them.
Reporting a problem needs description rather than a memorised phrase. Get to it.
Ask the questions a real desk asks, including unprepared ones.
Vary the hotel, the room number and the small talk each time.

target_vocabulary: to check in, to check out
a single room, a double room
suggested_vocabulary: a towel, a pillow, a blanket
it does not work, it is broken
the bill, an extra charge, the minibar
the gym, the pool, the car park
target_grammar: numbers for nights, floors, room numbers and times
describing a problem: it is, it does not, there is no
past forms for what happened in the room

scenarios.name: A straightforward check-in
scenarios.description: Reservation, details, key, directions to the room.

scenarios.name: The room is not ready
scenarios.description: The student has to ask what to do and where to wait.

scenarios.name: Asking about breakfast
scenarios.description: Times, location, whether it is included.

scenarios.name: Asking about wifi
scenarios.description: The student asks for the code and reads it back.

scenarios.name: Something is wrong with the room
scenarios.description: The student describes a problem and asks for it to be sorted.

phases.name: Checking in
phases.purpose: Arriving at the desk: check-in please, I have a reservation, giving your name, handing over a passport.
instructions: The role-play is the front desk as they arrive.
advancement_guidance: You have a rough sense of their level with this.

phases.name: Your room
phases.purpose: Understanding what the desk tells you: the room, the key, which floor, how many nights.
instructions: The role-play is the receptionist giving them their room.

activities.name: Spelling a name
activities.description: The student spells their surname aloud in the target language.

entry_guidance: Skip most of this if the student is comfortable.
advancement_guidance: They can open a check-in unaided.

phases.name: Asking about the hotel
phases.purpose: Asking what time breakfast is, whether there is wifi, and for the password.
instructions: The role-play is the student asking the desk questions.
advancement_guidance: The student opens and sustains the exchange without prompts.

phases.name: Check-in, start to finish
phases.purpose: The whole arrival at the desk, using everything so far.
instructions: Play the receptionist. Use only what the student has been taught.

activities.name: Arrival end to end
activities.description: From greeting to being handed the key.

activities.name: The room is not ready
activities.description: An unexpected wait the student must respond to.

phases.name: Something is wrong
phases.purpose: Reporting a problem with the room: something does not work, there is no hot water.
instructions: The role-play is calling the front desk.

activities.name: What does the hotel have?
activities.description: Breakfast, wifi, gym, parking, check-out time.

advancement_guidance: The student asks several questions unprompted.

phases.name: Checking out
phases.purpose: Checking out, asking them to keep your luggage, thanking them.
instructions: The role-play is the desk on the last morning.

activities.name: Describing the problem
activities.description: The student explains what is wrong and what they want done.

entry_guidance: This is the most valuable phase. Reach it if you can.
advancement_guidance: The problem was described and a resolution agreed.

phases.name: The whole stay
phases.purpose: Arrival, one question, one problem and checking out, using everything so far.
instructions: Play the receptionist. Use only what the student has been taught.

activities.name: Settling the bill
activities.description: Key returned, charges checked, payment made.

phases.name: Review
phases.purpose: Everything from this lesson, from memory.
instructions: Ask for each thing from its English.
Then say what they can now do.
completion_guidance: End on something they did well.

if_struggling: Stay in the guided phase and reduce the exchange to one question at a time.
Offer a choice of two answers rather than an open question.
Drop the unexpected questions and keep the check-in predictable.
Skip the problem phase entirely; describing a fault is demanding.
Repeat the same check-in with a different name and number of nights.
if_succeeding: Ask questions they cannot have prepared for.
Move to the problem phase early and make the problem awkward.
Put a disputed charge on the bill.
Have the phone ring mid-conversation so the exchange is interrupted and resumed.

basis: whether a check-in and a check-out have both been handled unaided
progress.notes: Approximate. Never state a percentage to the student.

criteria: the student has checked in unaided
the student has asked at least two questions about the hotel without prompting
announcement_guidance: Mention the problem description specifically if they got that far — it is the hardest part.

observe: hotel and accommodation vocabulary produced unprompted
whether spelling aloud and numbers were reliable
how well the student described a problem
memory.notes: Ordinary vocabulary and weakness observations for the student's existing memory.
